Bajaj Qute

By: Chuma Kave | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Summary:
Bajaj e-hailers have been promised hell if they enter certain areas with their cars to pick up or drop off customers. Actually, Bajaj is not classified as a car but a quadricycle and recently a number of them got impounded by the JMPD due to them not being in possession of operator’s licenses. Some drivers are now operating in fear. The E-hailing industry regards them as a big disaster waiting to happen as they consider them unsafe and not fast enough to escape violence that could be unleashed on them and the mini-bus taxi industry commented that “we don’t even want to see those things here”. Bajaj Qute is a quadricycle originally from India that has been introduced to the e-hailing industry by Bolt South Africa. It is regarded as the most affordable for consumers and drives at a top speed of 70km per hour. It is supposed to take trips not more than 4km with only one passenger.

The E-hailing industry association believes the introduction of Bejaj into the market is just another exploitation by the big apps and they swear that Bejaj won’t last in South Africa. They believe that these cars will be abused on the road and will leave a number of drivers with a huge debt. The Bejaj is an improved version of a Tuk-Tuk and even though  Tuk-Tuks are located in limited areas, it seems the Bejaj will be able to move around the city. The Bajaj has been approved by the SA regulator, The National Regulator for Compulsory Specifications (NRCS) as it meets the specification of a quadricycle.
To acquire a Bajaj for Bolt, a driver pays R1500 a week for 3 years. The company supplying Bejaj, MyNextCar, takes care of the insurance and maintenance. On our visit to MyNextCar offices,  a long queue of drivers was signing up for a car that even its own industry, the ehailing industry, believes is not welcomed in South Africa. They feel the app giant is just adding a problem on top of all the other problems they are experiencing. 

What is Bajaj and can it survive the South Africa tough and hostile e-hailing industry?

BAJAJ QUTE Final

1. VO: It’s an almost comical sight on Johannesburg roads… a peculiar little yellow carrier, ambling along the northern suburbs…

Link Claire: It’s small in size, economical and if you ask those in the e-hailing taxi business, it’s already punching above it’s weight… 

2. This is the Bajaj Qute… In July this year motorists and commuters were baffled, by this nifty new arrival

3. VO: Not even a week on the market and Khathu Mathivha jumped at the opportunity to get into the minuscule Qute… becoming an e-hailing driver.

Upsound: Hi Khathu. Claire…
Claire: Is it even a car?
Khathu: Yes, with a motorbike engine.

4. VO: But, contrary to what Khathu might say, The Qute, isn’t actually a car. With a top speed of just 70kms per hour… it is in fact, a rear-engine, four-passenger quadricycle…

5. VO: Ten years ago, the Qute entered the market in India – where it’s also not classified as a car – its closest cousin is the Tuk-TuK…

Upsound Claire: So, this is your office. Is it a comfortable office?
Upsound Khathu: it’s very to me… It’s not that bad. Bad. Bad. We normally do 1 km, and 3 km around.

6: VO: The Qute has been introduced by the e-hailing app Bolt - it provides their cheapest ride for trips, of no more than 4km. Drivers in the program pay a weekly rental fee of R1500 for three years, on a lease-to-own deal through MyNextCar.

7. VO: Light on fuel, Khathu pays a little over R200 for a full tank… and a little really does go a long way…

viz: Petrol station

8. VO: But as much as it’s a beacon of hope for drivers and budget-conscious passengers, the Qute hasn't been as well received by taxi and e-hailing drivers.

Taxi driver vx pop: the Bajaj is a problem. They must get off the road and they are not needed in South Africa.
Taxi patrol car vx pop: They no longer use the app. They call for customers. What they are doing is totally wrong!


9: As if surviving Joburg's pothole-ridden roads weren't enough of a challenge, Qute drivers are increasingly targeted by the opposition.

Viz: Damaged cars

10. VO: In a makeshift rank in bustling Randburg, Qute drivers have found themselves thrust into an impromptu alliance as tensions with the taxi industry simmer.

Upsound Driver: About 15 men came in a Quantum carrying sjamboks and beat us up… Took my phone and took my money….


11: it's a baffling response to a service the Bajaj drivers say poses little threat.


Upsound Claire: So you say you are supporting the taxi industry?

Upsound Khathu: we’re not even taking their customer. We make their businesses easier. We take people from their houses and we drop them by the taxi rank.

Claire: What do you think can be done to make sure that Bajaj drivers are safer?
Upsound Khathu: We understand the taxi industry also doing business e-hailing people are also doing business, but we need maybe government to intervene

12: By August tempers flared outside Wits University as a Qute driver was dropping a customer and a taxi association patrol car tried to block his way. ….Campus security was called in to intervene.

13:The patrol car’s branding pointed to the Faraday Taxi Association ………We find the association’s spokesperson Sihle Makhanya at their headquarters.

Upsound: Sihle Makhanya: We are not happy at all. The Bajajes are taking our jobs. There are laws we as the taxi industry have to follow that are route-based.

14: It’s the lack of consultation whenever government introduces a new mode of transport, that really gets to them.

Upsound Sihle: The government didn’t call us to say now we are introducing the new mode of transport.
Claire: The Bajaj drivers say you are attacking them.
Upsound Sihle: Let’s not call it an attack…call it something else.
Upsound Claire: The Bajaj drivers say it’s violent.
Upsound Sihle: That might be caused by the reaction at the first stage of the thing…if you say to them don’t load here.
Claire: You just don’t want Bajaj?
Upsound: Sihle: Completely

15: Back in Randburg, I find the drivers on the road, awaiting trips….But, their counterparts from other e-hailing services are not thrilled.

Upsound: Vhatuka: So when you introduce a cheaper service in a price-sensitive price market…you are creating a false opportunity and you are also creating a situation whereby there will be violent eruptions.

16: Vhatuka Mbelengwa represents the National E-Hailing Association – a market squeezed for profit.

Upsound Claire: What would you say then to all the current Bolt drivers who are driving Bajaj…that feel like this is an opportunity for them?

Vhatuka: The opportunity is not real. It will not live past 2024….We are going to find that this is going to produce more dead black children as a result of this false opportunity because they have been thrown into an unregulated environment….You can already see it now. Attacks, cars being turned over.

Claire: But it was happening to e-haling taxis long before the Bajaj
Vhatuka: Yes it was, but the situation is being compounded by continually adding people within a space where there isn't enough money flowing around…does make sense to add more into the industry

Link: “Since these little …uuuuum vehicles… have been on our roads, a number of them have been impounded… but somehow, it seems there’s ==many more of them already on our roads.”

17. As it gains popularity among customers, the big question is: Is it safe on the road?

18. In 2016 the Euro N-CAP scored it one star out of five in crash tests …and a meagre 28% for adult occupant safety.

Viz: car.co.za

19: Bolt, Bajaj South Africa and MyNext Car insist it’s eligible for our roads. But the National Regulator for Compulsory Specifications  says while it approved the quadricycle for road use - it didn’t for public transport…. Several QUTES have been impounded for operating without a license and yet they carry a double disc - which according to MyNextCar means, they can operate as taxis.

VIz: NRCS logo
Viz: Impounded cars

20: The Gauteng Traffic Police disagrees.
Upsound Sello: Doesn't matter whether they had a double disc or what. It’s a requirement on its own. It has nothing to do with the operating license issued in terms of the National Land Transport Act five of 2009, your disc is issued in terms of your National Road Traffic Act 93 of 1996. So are we talking different legislations here.
21: Spokesperson SELLO MAREMANE says after impounding the vehicles in August BOLT took them to court.
Upsound Sello: Their court case was dismissed. We won the case against them. All of those vehicles that we have impounded, we charge them 5000 rand.
22: He insists they are not complying and promises EVEN more action.
Upsound Sello: If you look at that vehicle…they’re just not fit for public transport usage
Link: Having spent time with a number of Bajaj Bolt drivers and hearing from the other side, clearly something needs to done. Soon! We don’t need another tragedy for a “Wake Up Call” (3328)

23: Dealing with potholes, taxis, and e-hailing competition, QUTE drivers are hopeful that industry issues will settle, and law enforcement will ensure their protection - like any other driver.

Viz: What would you like motorists to know about the Bajaj?

Claire: It’s just a car. Keep left, pass right






PROMO 1
VO: It’s small, cramped, with absolutely no legroom. The Bajaj Qute is the new e-hailing service that has taken Joburg by storm…

Upsound Claire: Is this even a car?
Upsound Khathu: It’s a car with an engine of a motorbike

VO:…and is facing a storm.
Upsound Sihle:…they are taking our jobs.

PROMO 2
VO: It’s an industry under siege. Bajaj Qute e-haling drivers are working in a cloud of fear and daily intimidation.

Upsound Khathu: We are not taking their customers. We are actually making their business becomes easier.

PROMO 3
VO: A peculiar sight in the suburbs of Joburg. The yellow Bajaj Qute e-hailing service has hit the streets… and some want it gone.

Upsound taxi driver: They must get out. They are no needed in South Africa
